input: Given question: A patient visits you complaining of decreased deltoid function. You conclude that they have suffered damage to their axillary nerve. The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space, the lateral border of which is formed by the humerus. What forms the medial border? Option A: Inferior border of subscapularis Option B: Inferior border of teres minor Option C: Long head of triceps brachii Option D: Short head of biceps brachii Option E: Superior border of teres major The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Inferior borders of subscapularis and teres minor – form the superior border Long head of triceps brachii – forms medial border Short head of biceps brachii – does not form a border of the quadrangular space Superior border of teres major – forms inferior border
best_explanation:
Humerus  Radius  Ulna  Inferior border of subscapularis Inferior border of teres minor  Long head of triceps brachii  Short head of biceps brachii  Superior border of teres major  Deltoid  Rotator cuff  Surrounding tissue  Axillary nerve  Brachial artery  Veins  C5, C6, C7 roots of brachial plexus  C5, C6, C7 axillary nerve forms the superior border of the quadrangular space while the long head of triceps brachii forms the lateral border.  The axillary nerve is the most likely nerve to be damaged in axillary nerve injury which may result in decreased deltoid function.  Brachial artery also passes through the quadrangular space.  The quadrangular space is a compartment within the deltoid which contains the axillary nerve, brachial artery, veins and the rotator cuff muscles (supracrustocervicalis).  The quadrangular space is innervated by the axillary nerve.  The quadrangular space is an important anatomical region as damage to the axillary nerve or the surrounding tissue may have implications on the function of the deltoid, rotator cuff and the overall function of the shoulder joint.  The quadrangular space can be assessed by a healthcare professional by palpation.

input: Given question: A patient comes into clinic complaining of an inability to move their wrist resulting in a 'wrist drop'. The patient also complains of a loss of sensation in some of the skin in the forearm. What nerve has the patient likely to have damaged? Option A: Median Nerve Option B: Ulnar Nerve Option C: Radial Nerve Option D: Musculocutaneous Nerve Option E: Medial pectoral nerve The correct answer is Option C.
reference: The radial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the upper limb. As such it innervates the muscles responsible for extension of the wrist and fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Hence the patient is unable to extend the wrist.
best_explanation: Damage to the radial nerve results in a 'wrist drop' and sensory loss over the dorsal surface of the forearm. This is because the radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the wrist and the posterior forearm. These muscles are responsible for extending the wrist and therefore when the nerve is damaged the wrist flexor dominates and 'wrist drop' results. The sensory loss is due to the radial nerve innervating the dorsal surface of the forearm.  A) Median Nerve- responsible for innervating the anterior surface of the forearm and the flexor muscles of the wrist. Damage to this nerve results in ' claw hand' where the patient is unable to flex the wrist and the fingers are permanently bent into a claw shape. B) Ulnar Nerve- responsible for innervating the medial surface of the forearm and the flexor muscles of the hand. Damage to this nerve results in 'hand of Benediction' where the patient is unable to flex the wrist, the hand appears to be in a fist with the little finger elevated. C) Musculocutaneous nerve- responsible for innervating the lateral surface of the forearm and the flexor muscles of the upper arm. Damage to this nerve results in 'biceps curl' where the patient is unable to extend the wrist and the hand is permanently bent into a flexed position. D) Medial pectoral nerve- this nerve innervates the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles in the chest. E) Made up nerve- doesn't exist (I hope!) but it was included to throw you off the scent!  References:McCarthy, D. (2012). Clinical Relevance of the Upper Limb. In Anatomy and Physiology of the Upper Limb (2nd ed.). OUP. pp. 261-262.

input: Given question: Martha is suffering from the early stages of heart failure whereby her heart is beginning to be less effective but her neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms mean that she has few symptoms. At a routine check up, her GP notices that her resting heart rate has increased since her last check up, which the GP puts down to this compensatory response. Which of the following neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms is responsible for this increase? Option A: Endothelin pathway activation Option B: Left ventricular hypertrophy Option C: Parasympathetic inhibition Option D: RAAS activation Option E: Sympathetic stimulation The correct answer is Option E.
reference: The sympathetic nervous system is activated. This acts to increase heart rate and contractility in order to increase cardiac output and blood pressure. However, this increases the workload and oxygen demand of the heart which can cause decompensation if it worsens the left ventricular dysfunction. A (endothelin pathway activation) - This increases blood pressure by vasoconstrictionB (left ventricular hypertrophy) - This increases the mass of the muscle making up the left ventricleC (parasympathetic inhibition) - Not a direct neurohormonal response to heart failureD (RAAS activation) - This increases blood pressure by salt and water retention and other methodsE (sympathetic stimulation) - CORRECT The compensatory responses to heart failure increase the workload of the heart, leading to decompensation, which causes a spiral of heart failure. This was covered in the case 12 lecture ‘CARDIAC FAILURE: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY, PRESENTATION & INVESTIGATION’.
best_explanation: In heart failure, there is a decreased parasympathetic drive and an increased sympathetic drive, which acts to increase the resting heart rate. This is part of the neurohormonal compensation that occurs early on in heart failure. Activation of the endothelin pathway, left ventricular hypertrophy, RAAS activation and parasympathetic inhibition are all downstream effects of this sympathetic stimulation.  Source: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, 9e.  This was covered in the case 12 lecture ‘HAEMATOLOGICAL ISSUES IN CARDIAC FAILURE’.   (For those who are interested, the increase in resting heart rate in heart failure is mostly due to an increase in sympathetic drive. This is because there is an increase in the number of sympathetic nerve endings in the heart and surrounding areas in heart failure, which act to increase beating rate. This is a compensatory mechanism as it tries to increase cardiac output in order to maintain organ perfusion. However, as the heart becomes less effective, it is unable to compensate for the increased sympathetic drive and so the resting heart rate increases.    For more information, see Case 12, Lecture 4 - ‘Neurohormonal Mechanisms’.)   This was covered in the case 12 lecture ‘HAEMATOLOGICAL ISSUES IN CARDIAC FAILURE’. reference: This patient has a GCS of 6. This indicates airway management is needed as GCS is less than 8. A CT scan may well be needed however the airway is a more urgent concern. DC cardioversion may also be needed however not enough information is given here to indicate it.
